title: Mammals radiate after the dinosaurs' extinction

facts.text: With the non-avian dinosaurs gone, mammals rapidly increased in size and diversity and filled the emptied niches.
The K–Pg extinction had wiped out every land animal heavier than about 25 kg, leaving many niches open at the start of the Paleocene.
Many crown placental groups arose, including the earliest afrotherians, xenarthrans, rodents, carnivorans and the primate forerunners called plesiadapiforms.
Most Paleocene mammals stayed small, under about 20 kg, until near the end of the epoch.
Mammals have been the dominant land animals ever since, a shift that eventually set the stage for humans.

image.caption: Momotarou2012, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts.text: Four bird lineages survived the K–Pg extinction: the ostrich group, waterfowl, ground fowl and Neoaves, the ancestors of most living birds.
Surviving modern birds diversified rapidly at the start of the Paleogene, filling niches left by extinct Mesozoic bird groups.
It was one of the fastest diversifications of any group; modern bird groups had likely split within about four million years.
Nearly all modern bird lineages except fowl and palaeognaths trace their origins to the Paleocene, according to DNA studies.
Paleocene bird fossils are scarce and mostly waterbirds; the earliest known tree-dwelling crown bird, the mousebird Tsidiiyazhi, dates to about 62 Ma.
An asteroid at least 400 m wide struck the seafloor on the Guinea Plateau, off Guinea-Bissau, leaving a crater about 9.2 km across.
It formed at or near the K–Pg boundary, around the same time as Chicxulub; the age is uncertain by about a million years.
The impact would have raised tsunami waves up to 1 km high and released greenhouse gases from buried black shales.
Pantodonts, herbivorous mammals, were among the first large mammals to evolve after the end of the Cretaceous.
The earliest pantodonts, such as dog-sized Bemalambda, appear in the early Paleocene Shanghuan Formation of China.
In North America they appear in the middle Paleocene and grew larger through the epoch; Barylambda was the largest Paleocene form.

title: Corral Bluffs and the earliest Paleocene mammal fauna

facts.text: Colorado's Denver Formation holds one of the world's most diverse earliest Paleocene mammal faunas, recording mammal diversification right after the K–Pg extinction.
Its rocks span the latest Cretaceous to the early Paleocene, before, during and after the boundary event.
Its Danian Corral Bluffs locality yields new species such as the alligator relative Mandrasuchus.

title: Earliest undisputed placental mammals

facts.text: The oldest undisputed placental mammal fossils come from the early Paleocene, just after the non-avian dinosaurs died out.
The earliest known placental and marsupial mammals are recorded from the Paleocene, though most Paleocene mammals have uncertain relationships.
The first Paleocene land mammal age (Puercan) brought taeniodonts, early hoofed 'condylarths' and possible primate relatives such as Purgatorius.
Placentals, marsupials and monotremes all originated in the Cretaceous, before their fossils become common.

title: Multituberculates peak, then decline

facts.text: Multituberculates, rodent-like mammals that were the most successful Mesozoic mammals, reached their peak diversity in the early Paleocene.
European and North American forms bounced back quickly after the K–Pg event, but Asian forms were devastated.
They declined from the middle Paleocene, probably outcompeted by placental mammals such as rodents and ungulates.

title: Alpine collision begins as Piemont-Liguria Ocean closes

facts.text: By the Paleocene the Piemont-Liguria Ocean had fully subducted under the Apulian plate, and Apulia began colliding with Europe.
This collision would go on to raise the Alps and the Apennines.
The Briançonnais microcontinent then arrived at the subduction zone.
Africa, Arabia and India had long been converging on Eurasia, but the major phases of Alpine mountain building began in the Paleocene to Eocene.
Alpine stresses uplifted the Sudetes and may have faulted rocks as far away as Öland in Sweden.

title: Great Paleocene coal swamps form

facts.text: Several major coal deposits formed in the Paleocene, including the Fort Union Formation, which yields 43% of American coal, Texas's Wilcox Group and Colombia's Cerrejón.
Powder River Basin coal began forming about 60 Ma as the land rose out of a shallow sea.
In Wyoming, thick coal beds built up as eroding highlands buried plant matter.

title: Laramide uplift of the Rocky Mountains

facts.text: The Laramide orogeny, which began in the Late Cretaceous, kept raising the Rocky Mountains through the Paleocene.
It deformed the crust deeply, from Canada to northern Mexico, in pulses separated by quiet phases.
The Denver Basin deepened between 66 and 45 million years ago as the uplift built the Colorado Rockies.
Together with the collapse of the continental borderland, it reversed the course of the California River.
By one account it ended at the end of the Paleocene; other sources place its end between 55 and 35 million years ago and call the timing disputed.

facts.text: An impact in what is now Ukraine left the Boltysh crater, 24 km across.
Argon–argon dating in 2021 places it in the Danian, about 650,000 years after the Chicxulub impact.
That study suggested the impact may have disrupted recovery from the K–Pg extinction and could explain a fern spike.

facts.text: Early in the Danian, the Dan-C2 event brought about 100,000 years of rising carbon, especially in the deep sea.
It may have released carbon stored in the deep sea since the mid-Maastrichtian once deep water warmed past a threshold, or followed a pulse of Deccan volcanism.
It sits at the very base of the Cenozoic, the first of the early Paleogene hyperthermals.
South America's native hoofed mammals, such as notoungulates and litopterns, appeared in the early Paleocene, around 65–63 Ma, probably from North American 'condylarth' ancestors.
They lasted until the end of the Pleistocene, about 12,000 years ago; litopterns, for example, appear around 62.5 Ma.
Ancient proteins show litopterns were true ungulates, related to today's horses, rhinos and tapirs.

conflicts.note: Notoungulata page: estimated divergence date

facts.text: Plesiadapiforms, early relatives or forerunners of primates, first appear in the fossil record between 65 and 55 Ma; many were gone by the Eocene.
Purgatorius, a possible primate relative, is among the new mammals of the first Paleocene mammal age, though it may sit outside primates.
Plesiadapiforms diversified in North America from about 65.1 Ma and may be the earliest mammals with fingernails instead of claws.
Timelines place the first true primates around 60 Ma.

facts.text: The Baunekule facies of Denmark's Faxe Formation preserves an exceptionally well-preserved cold-water coral mound ecosystem from 64–63 million years ago.
The mounds were dominated by Dendrophyllia corals and also hold gastropods, tubeworms, bivalves and bryozoans.
Creodonts, an important group of meat-eating mammals, evolved about 63 Ma.
The earliest oxyaenids appear in North America's Tiffanian age, from about 62.3 Ma.
Hyainailouroid hyaenodonts probably evolved in Afro-Arabia during the late Paleocene.

title: Main phase of Deccan volcanism ends

facts.text: The bulk of the Deccan lavas erupted from fissures in the Western Ghats between 66 and 65 Ma; two-thirds may have formed within a million years around 65.5 Ma.
India's plate motion slowed around 63 Ma, by which time the main phase of Deccan volcanism had ended.
The Latest Danian Event (Top Chron C27n Event) lasted about 200,000 years and warmed the whole water column by 1.6–2.8 °C.
It came with rising carbon and ocean acidification, during major Atlantic seafloor spreading and volcanism off southeast Greenland.
Egypt's Qreiya 3 site, laid down in oxygen-poor seas after the event, holds over 500 articulated fish fossils.

facts.text: The first penguins, Crossvallia and Kupoupou, appear around 62 Ma in Antarctica and New Zealand, the earliest known birds built for life in water.
The early penguin Waimanu is one of the few Paleocene bird fossils.
Penguins about 2 m tall lived from about 60 to 30 Ma.

title: North America's inland sea drains away

facts.text: The Western Interior Seaway, which had joined the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean since about 100 Ma, lasted into the earliest Paleocene.
In the early Paleocene a remnant still flooded the Mississippi Embayment, over the site of Memphis.
Around 62 Ma, falling sea level and retreating inland seas completed the emergence of North America.

title: Seafloor spreading opens the Labrador Sea

facts.text: Seafloor spreading pushed north from the Central Atlantic between North America and Greenland, opening the Labrador Sea around 62 Ma and Baffin Bay around 57 Ma.
The opening split the North Atlantic Craton, a block of ancient crust shared by Labrador and Greenland.
Spreading reached the northern Labrador Sea as Greenland slid past Ellesmere Island.
By 56 Ma Greenland had become a separate plate, cut off from North America by the Labrador Sea–Baffin Bay rift.
By the early Eocene, about 54 Ma, spreading had moved into the northeast Atlantic between Greenland and Eurasia.

facts.text: Around the Danian–Selandian boundary, oxygen-poor water spread into coastal seas.
Sea level dropped, most likely through warming and evaporation, since no polar ice existed to lock up water.
It is counted among the early Paleogene hyperthermal events.

facts.text: A mantle plume, ancestor of today's Iceland hotspot, rose beneath Greenland around 65 Ma.
Its most active magmatism ran from about 60.5 to 54.5 Ma, in a pre-break-up phase (62–58 Ma) and a break-up phase (56–54 Ma).
It was the third-largest magmatic event of the last 150 million years, roughly 5 million cubic km of rock from Canada and Greenland to Britain.
It built flood basalts on Baffin Island and the last volcanic rocks of the British Isles, formed between 63 and 52 Ma.
Volcanism on Greenland's southeast margin coincided with the Latest Danian warming around 62.2 Ma.

facts.text: Carnivoramorphs, the group that includes today's carnivorans, first appeared in North America about 60 Ma, 6 million years after the K–Pg extinction.
The earliest carnivorans, such as Ravenictis and Pristinictis, are Paleocene; the miacids, ancestors of later carnivores, evolved around 60 Ma.

facts.text: Proboscideans, the elephant order, first evolved in Africa around 60 Ma, during the Selandian.
The earliest known, Eritherium, weighed only about 3–8 kg.

title: High Arctic Large Igneous Province falls silent

facts.text: The High Arctic Large Igneous Province, active since 130 Ma, ended around 60 Ma.
Its second phase, from about 85 to 60 Ma, brought mildly alkaline magmatism and flood basalts.
It covers over 1,000,000 km², one of the largest magmatic complexes on Earth.

title: India begins colliding with Eurasia

facts.text: India, racing north since the Late Cretaceous, had begun its collision with Asia by the Paleocene.
One account dates the India–Eurasia collision to the middle Paleocene, about 60 Ma, starting the Himalayan orogeny.
Southern Tibet's Gangdese batholith reawakened around 65 Ma as India approached and stayed active for 20 million years.
Between about 60 and 50 Ma, the leading edge of Greater India struck the West Burma block.
The size of Greater India and the timing of collision are debated; models range from late Paleocene contact to collision in the middle Eocene.

contested_note: The sources describe a debate over the timing and nature of the India–Eurasia collision, with dates from about 65 Ma to the middle Eocene.

facts.text: Colombia's Cerrejón Formation, about 60–58 Ma, holds the earliest record of Neotropical rainforest, on a wet coastal plain near 5°N.
Titanoboa, which lived there, grew over 13 m long, the longest snake ever recorded; a 60-million-year-old Colombian turtle, Carbonemys, had a 1.7 m shell.
A snake that size implies mean annual temperatures of 30–34 °C, though leaf-based estimates run 6–8 °C cooler.
Its plants already belonged to modern rainforest families such as palms, legumes and aroids.
Low plant diversity and unspecialized insect damage show the forest was still recovering from the K–Pg extinction 7 million years later.

title: Izanagi–Pacific ridge sinks beneath East Asia

facts.text: At the start of the Paleogene, the Pacific Ocean floor was made of the Pacific, Farallon, Kula and Izanagi plates.
Between 60 and 50 Ma, the Izanagi–Pacific spreading ridge began to be subducted beneath East Asia.
Little Izanagi sea floor survives, so the history of that margin is poorly known.

title: Late Paleocene cooling and transient ice

facts.text: From 59.7 to 58.1 Ma, burial of organic carbon cooled the climate, lowered sea level and allowed brief ice growth.
The icing of Antarctica may have begun as early as the late Paleocene, between 60 and 45.5 Ma.
Other evidence finds no significant ice sheets or sea ice from the late Paleocene into the early Eocene.

title: Horned dinoceratans appear

facts.text: Dinocerata, large hoofed plant-eaters with horns and tusk-like canines, appear in the late Paleocene.
Early forms such as Prodinoceras appear almost at once in North America and Asia, implying a land link, probably Beringia.
Near the end of the Tiffanian age, uintatheres immigrated to North America from Asia.

title: Rodents and rabbits appear

facts.text: Lagomorphs, the rabbit order, appear in the late Paleocene and may have evolved in India while it was an island continent.
The earliest rodents, such as Tribosphenomys and Paramys, are Paleocene.
Rodents immigrated from Asia to North America in the Clarkforkian age, from about 57.5 Ma.

title: Thulean land bridge links Europe and North America

facts.text: A land bridge, now sunk beneath the Atlantic, appeared in the late Paleocene and linked the British Isles to Greenland, and so Europe to North America.
The Thulean route was open around 57 and 55.8 Ma; Beringia linked North America and Asia at 65.5 and 58 Ma.
It disappeared in the early Eocene.

facts.text: Around 59 Ma, just before the Selandian–Thanetian boundary, temperatures spiked, probably from a mass release of deep-sea methane hydrate.
It and a second pulse 300,000 years later (MPBE-2) released about 83 and 132 billion tonnes of methane-derived carbon, suggesting 2–3 °C of warming.
At Itzurun, Spain, it shows as a dark 1 m layer poor in calcium carbonate.

title: Long warming toward the Eocene hothouse begins

facts.text: From the late Paleocene through the early Eocene, about 58 to 50 Ma, Earth warmed over the long term, punctuated by hyperthermals.
Surface temperatures rose gradually by about 6 °C over that span.
The relatively cool late Paleocene ended with the Thanetian Thermal Event and then the PETM.
Global mean surface temperature in the latest Paleocene, about 57 Ma, is estimated at 22.3–28.3 °C.
Plant diversity at both poles rose through the Paleocene, especially at its end, as the world warmed.
A metallic asteroid about 1.5 km wide left a 31 km crater now buried under Greenland's Hiawatha Glacier.
Argon–argon and uranium–lead dating of zircons in its melt rock give 57.99 ± 0.54 Ma, in the late Paleocene.
The impact has no clear climatic effects, and its age rules out a link to the Younger Dryas.

facts.text: At the end of the Paleocene, about 2,500–4,500 billion tonnes of carbon poured into the air and oceans, spiking temperatures and acidifying the sea.
Global average temperature rose about 5–8 °C during an event lasting about 200,000 years; mid-latitude and polar regions may have topped today's tropical temperatures.
Proposed carbon sources include magma sills baking organic-rich sediments in the North Atlantic Igneous Province, seafloor methane clathrates and kimberlite eruptions at Lac de Gras, Canada.
Its onset may have taken anywhere from a few decades to several thousand years.
It wiped out 30–50% of deep-sea benthic foraminifera, which had come through the K–Pg extinction unscathed, and is linked to one of the smaller mass extinctions.
